nameStory: The Pinewood Gingertail gets its charming name from its golden-orange coloration that resembles the warm hue of fresh ginger root, especially visible on the stem base. The 'pinewood' part reflects its strong preference for growing on decaying coniferous wood, particularly pine logs and stumps. Some folks also call it the golden trumpet for its small, bell-shaped caps that seem to announce the arrival of cooler weather.
description: The Pinewood Gingertail is a delicate, small mushroom that grows in cheerful clusters on rotting coniferous wood. These tiny fungi rarely exceed an inch across, with thin, translucent caps that start bell-shaped and flatten with age, displaying beautiful golden-yellow to orange-brown colors. The slender stems often have a distinctive orange to reddish-brown base that gives the mushroom its 'gingertail' nickname. You'll typically find dozens growing together in overlapping troops on the same piece of decaying wood.

idTips.label: Stem Base
idTips.description: The stem base shows distinctive orange to reddish-brown coloration, often with fine fuzzy hairs - this 'gingery' colored base is the most reliable identifying feature

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Small translucent caps (0.5-1 inch) that are bell-shaped when young, flattening with age, colored golden-yellow to orange-brown with a slightly sticky feel when moist

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Widely spaced, pale yellow gills that run slightly down the stem, giving a delicate, almost lacy appearance underneath the cap

idTips.label: Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Always grows in dense, overlapping clusters or troops on coniferous wood, never singly - if you find one, look for dozens more nearby

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Produces a white spore print, though the tiny size makes this difficult to observe in the field

habitat: Look for Pinewood Gingertails on decaying coniferous logs, stumps, and fallen branches throughout New England's forests, particularly in areas with pine, spruce, and fir. They thrive in moist, shaded woodland areas where fallen wood has begun to soften and decay. You'll often find them in mixed forests at various elevations, from lowland woods to mountain slopes, wherever conifers are present.

seasonality.spring: Early clusters may appear on well-rotted logs as temperatures warm and spring rains provide moisture, though not the peak season.
seasonality.summer: Moderate fruiting continues through summer, especially after periods of rain when the wood substrate stays consistently moist.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for Pinewood Gingertails, with the largest and most numerous clusters appearing as cool, wet weather arrives and persists.
seasonality.winter: In milder winters or during warm spells, small clusters may persist or appear on well-sheltered, unfrozen logs.

funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, Pinewood Gingertails are remarkably cold-tolerant and can continue growing even when temperatures hover near freezing - they're among the few mushrooms you might find fruiting under a light dusting of snow!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small, clustered mushrooms on wood, but the distinctive orange-reddish stem base is your best clue. Remember: 'Ginger at the bottom, golden on top' - if the stem base lacks that warm ginger coloration, it's likely a different species entirely.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name 'campanella' means 'little bell' in Latin, referring to the characteristic bell-shaped young caps. This mushroom was formerly classified in the genus Omphalina, so you may still see it called 'bell Omphalina' in older field guides.
compareHints: Pinewood Gingertail differs from its relatives by consistently growing on coniferous wood rather than deciduous wood or soil. The Cross-veined Troop Mushroom has distinctive cross-veining on the gills that's visible with close inspection, while other Xeromphalina species lack the distinctive orange-reddish stem base coloration. The consistent clustering habit and conifer preference make this the most commonly encountered Xeromphalina in New England.
